answer.label: Not George Washington — actually William E. Borah
answer.sourceLine: This aphorism does not appear in any of George Washington’s writings, and his estate at Mount Vernon lists it among its “spurious quotations.” The Check Your Fact review ↗, citing Mount Vernon’s encyclopedia, traces the words to Idaho senator William E. Borah, credited with the line in a Reader’s Digest piece around 1929. The Washington credit is a later, unsupported reassignment.

source.heading: What the record shows
source.excerpt: The marvel of all history is the patience with which men and women submit to burdens unnecessarily laid upon them by their governments.
trail: The fact-check site Check Your Fact rates the Washington credit false and points to Senator William E. Borah ↗, citing Mount Vernon’s digital encyclopedia.
Quotation databases such as Goodreads ↗ and The Quotations Page ↗ file the line under Borah, not Washington.
George Washington’s Mount Vernon keeps a public list of spurious quotations ↗ for lines wrongly pinned on the first president.
source.excerptNote: No fuller original context has been located for the popular one-sentence form; it circulates as a standalone aphorism.

source.rightsNote: The wording is credited to Senator William E. Borah in a Reader’s Digest piece around 1929 (per Mount Vernon’s encyclopedia, as reported by Check Your Fact). As a U.S. work first circulated before 1931, that text is in the public domain in the United States. Note that this first-publication detail comes from secondary sources; the exact 1929 issue was not independently examined here.

author.name: William Edgar Borah
author.heading: About the real author
author.metaLine: 1865–1940 · U.S. Senator from Idaho & famed orator
author.bio: William Edgar Borah was a Republican U.S. senator from Idaho who served from 1907 until his death in 1940, earning the nickname “the Lion of Idaho.” A celebrated orator and leading isolationist, he was a central voice against the League of Nations and a frequent commentator on the reach of government — the milieu from which this line about citizens tolerating unnecessary burdens emerged.

misattribution.heading: Why the Washington credit is wrong
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good aphorism pinned on Washington because his name lends any anti-big-government line instant authority. The evidence points elsewhere.

items.why: The line appears in none of Washington’s writings and is catalogued on Mount Vernon’s spurious-quotations list ↗; the words are Senator William E. Borah’s.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Senator William E. Borah’s ↗, popularized through Reader’s Digest around 1929 and only later mis-stamped onto George Washington.

context.heading: Why it gets misattributed
lead: Short, quotable critiques of government are magnets for Washington’s name: attach it to the founding father and the line reads as timeless national wisdom rather than one 20th-century senator’s turn of phrase. That is exactly the pattern Mount Vernon built its ‘spurious quotations’ page to counter.

William Borah — a leading isolationist and one of the Senate’s most quoted orators — is the documented source, but his name lacks Washington’s marketing power online, so the misattribution keeps spreading.
context.pull: A senator’s aphorism, wearing a founding father’s name.
